result.summary: Brennus has bridges built over the Sperchius, bypasses Heraclea, and attacks the Greeks at Thermopylae. The Greeks, aided by Athenian triremes, repulse the furious but poorly armed Galati with heavy losses. Pausanias records the young Athenian Cydias' death and the Galati's indifference to burying their dead.

scenes.title: Brennus crosses the Sperchius
scenes.summary: Locals bridge the Sperchius for Brennus, who ravages Heraclea's land but cannot take the city, which the Ætolians protect.
scenes.stakes: Heraclea and the nearby Greeks risk being plundered by the barbarian army.

place.name: Sperchius and Heraclea
place.modern_name: Sperchios river valley, near Heraclea Trachinia

scenes.title: Battle at Thermopylae
scenes.summary: Brennus attacks the Greek force in the pass; the Greeks and Athenian ships drive the Galati back into the marsh in confusion.
scenes.stakes: The Greeks risk Brennus breaking into Greece; the Galati risk slaughter in the narrow pass.

scenes.title: Shield of Cydias
scenes.summary: Cydias' relatives dedicate his shield to Zeus Eleutherius at Athens; Sulla's soldiers later removed it.

scenes.title: After the battle
scenes.summary: The Greeks bury their dead while the Galati ignore theirs; Pausanias gives his reasons and the casualty figures.

alias_notes.explanation: Pausanias uses Celts and Galati for the same Gallic people.

notable_quotes.reason: Moving epitaph on a young soldier's shield dedicated to Zeus.
Vivid depiction of Galati ferocity, fighting like wild beasts.

analysis.text: The passage contrasts Greek discipline and terrain-aided tactics with barbarian fury, echoing earlier defenses of Thermopylae.
It describes the Gallic invasion of Greece in 279 BC, and Pausanias' note on Sulla reflects Roman plunder of Athens in 86 BC.

fun_facts.text: Pausanias suggests the Galati's neglect of burial was partly meant to terrify enemies, a view of Celtic custom he offers as opinion.

language_notes.text: The Sperchius is a river of Thessaly flowing into the Maliac Gulf; the "Maliac Bay" is that gulf, near Thermopylae.
The Ætolian League was a federation of Ætolian communities. Heraclea (Trachinia) was forced into it a year earlier, so Ætolians now defended it as their own.
"If indeed the Celts practise divination" is Pausanias' doubtful aside; Greek commanders normally consulted seers before battle.
"Light-armed troops" were unarmoured skirmishers using missiles, in contrast to the heavy infantry holding the line.
Zeus Eleutherius means "Zeus the Liberator"; his Athenian portico housed dedications commemorating wars for freedom.
Sulla, the Roman general, sacked Athens in 86 BC, and his soldiers carried off many treasures.

context_notes.text: Brennus led the Galati (Gauls) invading Greece in 279 BC, aiming for the rich sanctuary of Delphi.
The Athenian ships could approach because the sea at Thermopylae was shallow and silted, so movement was hard.
Cydias is known to us only through this account and his epitaph-like inscription.

literary_notes.text: Comparing the Galati to wild beasts emphasizes their ferocity and lack of discipline, contrasting with the orderly Greeks.
Trampling and men vanishing into the marsh vividly convey the rout's chaos.
The shield speaks in the first person, giving the dedication a mournful voice and underscoring Cydias' youth and loss.
Pausanias interjects his own opinion to explain Galatian customs, showing his habit of interpretation.
